title: Hybrid pool + probabilistic restitching: draft spec
content:
Purpose:
This note outlines a different approach to managing variable-length KV cached entries: a hybrid pool allocator combined with a probabilistic "restitching" background compaction process. The goal is to reduce long-term fragmentation without introducing large pause events or expensive full-table compactions. This is a working doc; design is intentionally incremental to allow experiments.

Background / motivation (short):
- Serving workload has wide variance in entry sizes (32B metadata to multi-kB context chunks).
- Existing slab-like designs reduce internal fragmentation but create many size-classes and complex eviction paths; compaction tends to be heavy.
- We observed persistent fragmentation under mixed steady+burst workloads in our sim runs (see linked experiments).

High-level goals:
- Keep allocation fast (amortized O(1) path for hot inserts).
- Bound tail latency introduced by background maintenance (<1 ms p95 for cache ops).
- Reduce steady-state wasted memory (target <10% fragmentation under mixed workloads).
- Make compaction incremental and NUMA-friendly; avoid global stop-the-world passes.

Constraints and trade-offs:
- GPU memory is page-aligned and large allocations are expensive; need to respect alignment and coalesce-friendly placement for large KV entries used in model caching.
- System runs on NUMA machines; prefer local pool affinity.
- Must interact with serving runtime's scheduling: compaction work should be throttled and preemptible.

Design overview (conceptual):
1) Hybrid pool layout:
   - Tiny pool: for entries <= 128B. Packed tightly; allocation via bump pointer within 4KB micro-pages. Fast free-list for reclaimed microblocks.
   - Compact pool: for 129B..4KB entries. Managed as a collection of variable-sized segments. Each segment contains a header with a compact free bitmap and an occupancy score.
   - Large pool: for >4KB entries. Allocated as whole pages/hugepages with direct mapping and optional explicit pinning.
   Pools are per-NUMA-node and per-serving-thread-group to reduce cross-node traffic.

2) Variable-length entry layout:
   - Each entry has a 16B header: 8B key-hash + 4B length + 4B flags (hot, pinned, tombstone, small-embedding).
   - Entries within the compact pool are stored back-to-back with a trailing 4B CRC. This keeps a simple parser for restitching.

3) Eviction policy (hybrid hot-size):
   - Primary rank = hotness_score (exponential decay LRU sample).
   - Secondary rank = size_penalty = log2(entry_size) * alpha. We penalize very large entries so they don't monopolize space when equally hot. Alpha is tunable per workload.
   - Tertiary: pinned flag and SLA tags (dedicated requests can pin entries).
   - Eviction tries within-pool first (evict from same pool/Numa region) before global demotion.

4) Probabilistic restitching (background compaction):
   - Idea: instead of scanning whole segments, we sample candidate segments with probability proportional to a fragmentation score.
   - Fragmentation score for segment S: F(S) = (free_bytes_in_holes / segment_capacity) * (1 + age_factor)
     where age_factor = min(1.0, seconds_since_last_compaction / 300).
   - Background worker wakes every 200ms (configurable) and picks N candidates (default N=4) using weighted reservoir sampling across local segments.
   - For each candidate segment we perform a lightweight restitch:
       a) Acquire per-segment compaction token (try-lock, fail -> skip).
       b) Scan for contiguous live runs and rebuild into a new target segment (allocated from the compact pool) until target is 80% filled or we've moved M entries (M tunable, default 128).
       c) Update in-place indirection entries (atomic pointers) to new locations; old slots are marked tombstones and reclaimed when all readers are done (epoch-based reclamation).
   - We probabilistically choose to continue or abort based on elapsed CPU time budget for this worker cycle (throttling).

5) Re-stitch cost model and heuristics:
   - Restitch only when expected reclaimed bytes > threshold T or expected reclaim/time > lambda. We compute expected reclaimed bytes from segment freelist stats.
   - Avoid moving very hot entries: if entry hotness > HOT_THRESHOLD exclude from move unless forced. This reduces write amplification and oscillation.

Fragmentation metrics we collect (prod + sim):
- external_fragmentation_pct = 1 - (sum_live_bytes / sum_allocated_bytes)
- average_gap_run_length
- compaction_work_per_second (bytes moved)
- compaction_p99_latency (time to finish a segment restitch)
- eviction_success_within_pool_pct

Simulator results (summary of runs on mix-8 workload, 64GB VM profile):
- baseline slab-multi-class (old): external_fragmentation=18.6% steady, compaction_work=1.2GB/s during bursts, 95th op latency 1.8ms.
- hybrid + probabilistic restitch (this doc): external_fragmentation=7.4% steady, compaction_work=140MB/s amortized, 95th op latency 0.95ms.
Notes: numbers are from our internal sim (linked PR) using synthetic mix derived from production traces (sampled keys, arrival distribution). These are promising but need more range tests (esp. extreme-all-large-entries).

Integration with scheduler and kernels:
- Background compaction is rate-limited by a token bucket keyed per-NUMA; token refill is proportional to free GPU cycles and a configable max_cpu_pct.
- Compaction worker yields when it detects heavy GPU kernel activity (we subscribe to a small performance counter from serving runtime: active_inference_kernels_count > K).
- To avoid contending with model kernels, compaction's atomic pointer updates are done with a low-priority CPU scheduling class (nice +19 equivalent in our task group).

Observability / debugging tools:
- Per-segment metrics: free_bytes, live_bytes, last_compaction_ts, compaction_attempts, compaction_successes.
- Export a "fragmentation heatmap" across NUMA nodes and pools; useful to see skew and decide on manual rebalancing.
- Add a /debug/compact/simulate endpoint that runs the restitcher in dry-run and reports predicted reclaimed bytes and moved-entry-count.

Open questions / risks:
- Indirection blowup: we rely on atomic indirection updates; if many readers retain old pointers this increases transient memory use. Need to bound epoch grace period.
- Hot-entry oscillation: moving hot entries may make them cold in new location; our exclusion heuristics mitigate but need validation.
- Large-entry starvation: with size_penalty eviction we may frequently evict large entries that are rare but expensive to recreate. Consider write-through hints or partial evict for huge entries.
- GPU pinned buffers: interactions for entries used directly by GPU (pinned mapping) complicate movement. For now, large/pinned entries are exempt from restitching and live in large-pool only.

Next steps / suggested experiments:
- Run sim with extreme-large-entry workload and with 10x arrival rate spikes to test compaction backpressure.
- Implement a minimal RESTITCHER in the sim branch (PR #842) and run on real trace day-by-day to compute operational token budgets.
- Microbench: measure p50/p95 of cache_get/cache_put under varying compaction token rate (0%, 1%, 5% CPU).

Immediate TODOs (for next sprint):
- [ ] Add per-segment compaction token (Jonah)
- [ ] Implement weighted reservoir sampling for candidate selection (Miguel)
- [ ] Hook compaction throttle into scheduler signals (Sara)

Notes to reviewer:
- This is deliberately conservative: restitching moves bounded batches and prefers sampling over scanning. The goal is to get fragmentation below 10% without new long pauses.
- Please check correctness around epoch-based reclamation and atomic pointer flips; I sketched it high-level but we need a concrete API for readers (RAII: CacheHandle with epoch pin).
